meta.title: The Confidence of the Lie Detector
meta.theme: why experience makes lie detectors more confident rather than more accurate
meta.learning_objective: decide what the last sentence must do, draw the consequence of the sentence before it, before reading the options

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General findings on lie detection accuracy; no specific text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: An early-tier completion: the paragraph builds to one claim (experience gives certainty, not accuracy) and the gap must draw its consequence. The stance-shift decoy is optimistic where the paragraph is sceptical.

quality.adversarial_review: The optimistic option about teaching lie detection is the strongest rival because it sounds like the kind of sentence a paragraph about a problem ends on. It fails on stance and support: the paragraph reports that experience does not improve accuracy and offers no evidence that training does, so a recommendation contradicts the paragraph's own scepticism. The 'harmless vanity' option contradicts the point sentence 4 is building toward: certainty without accuracy is exactly what makes the vanity costly.

sentences: Most people believe they are better than average at telling when someone is lying.
In controlled studies, however, the accuracy of untrained observers hovers just above chance, and the confident do no better than the hesitant.
Police officers, judges and customs agents, who might be expected to have learned from experience, score about the same as everyone else.
What experience gives them is not accuracy but certainty.

question.stem: Which of the following sentences best completes the paragraph?

options.A: This suggests that lie detection can be taught, provided the training concentrates on accuracy rather than on confidence.
options.B: Untrained observers, by contrast, tend to rely on facial cues that professionals have long learned to ignore.
options.C: The cost of that certainty is that a confident misjudgement is acted upon, while a hesitant one is checked.
options.D: Believing oneself a good judge of character is, after all, a common and largely harmless vanity.

explanation.what_the_gap_needs: The paragraph has just made its sharpest claim: experience produces certainty without accuracy. A closing sentence must draw the consequence of that claim, in the same sceptical register, at the same scope: professionals who judge lies. It must not introduce a remedy the paragraph has not earned, and it must not soften the point.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option takes 'certainty' from the last sentence and says why it matters: a confident misjudgement is acted upon, a hesitant one is checked. That is the consequence the paragraph has been building toward, it keeps the sceptical stance, and 'that certainty' ties it to the sentence before with a definite reference that nothing else in the paragraph could satisfy.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph is sceptical throughout and has just reported that experience does not improve accuracy; a hopeful claim that lie detection can be taught contradicts that stance and rests on nothing the paragraph offers.
distractors.seductive_element: Paragraphs about problems often end with a solution, and the phrase 'accuracy rather than confidence' echoes the last sentence.

distractors.why_wrong: Sentence 3 says professionals score about the same as untrained observers, so a contrast in which professionals have learned to ignore misleading cues contradicts the paragraph's own evidence.
distractors.seductive_element: 'By contrast' sounds like a paragraph developing its point, and facial cues are what everyone associates with lie detection.

distractors.why_wrong: The sentence before the gap has just shown why the vanity is not harmless, certainty without accuracy is exactly the problem, so a closing line calling it harmless reverses the paragraph's direction while sounding wise.
distractors.seductive_element: It is quotable and gently worldly, and 'after all' makes it sound like a conclusion.

explanation.method: Before reading the options, say what the last sentence has to do, here, draw the consequence of certainty without accuracy, and in what tone. Then test each option against that job. A sentence that changes the paragraph's stance, contradicts its evidence or sounds like a moral for a different paragraph is out, however elegant it is.

mentor.challenge: The paragraph stops one sentence early, just after its sharpest claim. Decide what that claim demands next before any option tries to decide for you.
mentor.takeaway: The last sentence does the job the sentence before it set up: never a new job.
